tactical_explanations:
**A) TSMC produces more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips, defined as those built at or below 7 nanometres.**

Paragraph 1 names TSMC as producing more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips and defines that class as chips built at or below 7 nanometres. The statement restates both the share and the process cutoff without adding or dropping a detail. Notice that the passage attaches the definition directly to the share with an appositive — "those built using process technologies at or below 7 nanometres" — so the 90% figure is scoped to that narrow class rather than to chips in general. A statement that kept the number but widened the category to all chips would fail even though the digits matched.

**Tip:** When a quantity and a definition travel together, both must match the passage.

The claim lines up with Paragraph 1's figure and definition, so it stands.

**B) A leading-edge fabrication plant now costs upward of $20 billion to construct.**

Paragraph 2 states that constructing a single leading-edge fab now costs upward of $20 billion. The statement only shortens that construction-cost claim; the number and direction ("upward of") are unchanged. "Upward of" sets a floor rather than a ceiling, so the statement's plain "costs upward of $20 billion" preserves the same open-ended direction the passage gives. Watch for versions of this line that convert the floor into a cap, such as "at most $20 billion," because that single preposition swap would break the match.

The $20 billion construction floor in Paragraph 2 confirms the line.

**C) Multiple companies worldwide currently manufacture the most advanced deep ultraviolet lithography machines, ensuring no single chokepoint exists for this equipment.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: only one company in the world, ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment, creating a second, narrower chokepoint. "Multiple companies" and "no single chokepoint" invert that monopoly. The passage is deliberate about scope: the monopoly claim covers "the most advanced version" of the equipment, which is exactly the tier the statement addresses, so there is no room to argue the two sentences describe different markets. Both halves of the statement — the supplier count and the reassuring conclusion drawn from it — contradict the text at once.

**Trap:** A true second-chokepoint fact is flipped into a diversified-supply claim.

The statement fails because Paragraph 2 limits advanced DUV lithography manufacture to ASML alone: "Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment."

**D) The rising capital cost of advanced fabs is described as making it easier for new companies to enter cutting-edge chip manufacturing.**

Paragraph 3 ties rising factory capital costs to Moore's Second Law and says those costs make it "progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge." "Easier" reverses the directional verb. The comparative adverb "progressively" matters too: the passage describes a barrier that keeps growing over time, which is the opposite of a market opening up to newcomers. Everything else in the statement — capital cost, new companies, cutting-edge manufacturing — is copied faithfully, which is precisely what makes the single reversed word easy to skim past.

**Trap:** Harder → easier is a classic polarity flip on cost barriers.

The claim fails; the passage says rising costs make entry "progressively harder," not easier.

**E) A single deep ultraviolet lithography machine can cost more than $150 million.**

Paragraph 2 states that a single deep ultraviolet lithography machine can cost more than $150 million. The statement copies that price ceiling without changing the equipment type or the figure. The modal "can cost" is preserved as well, so the claim reports a possible price point rather than asserting that every machine carries that tag. Keep this figure separate from the $20 billion fab total in the same paragraph, since the two numbers sit close together and are easy to swap under time pressure.

The $150 million machine-cost detail in Paragraph 2 matches the statement.

Constructing a single leading-edge fabrication plant, or "fab," now costs upward of $20 billion
Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment
making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge

tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2020–2021 chip shortage is attributed partly to a slowdown in a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips.**

Paragraph 4 opens the shortage discussion with "a production slowdown affecting a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips." The statement keeps that causal framing — a narrow automotive-grade category, not the whole market. The hedge "partly" is doing useful work here, because the passage presents the automotive slowdown as one exposed pressure point rather than the sole cause of everything that followed. Since the statement claims no more than the text does about scope or cause, nothing is overstated.

Paragraph 4's slowdown description supports the claim.

**B) This shortage is estimated to have reduced global vehicle production by roughly 11.3 million units.**

Paragraph 4 says the disruption ultimately reduced global vehicle production by an estimated 11.3 million units. "Roughly" is a fair hedge around "estimated"; the figure itself is unchanged. Softening an estimate with a word like "roughly" is safe, whereas hardening it into "exactly 11.3 million" would claim a precision the passage explicitly declines to give. Also check the unit: the passage counts vehicles, not chips or dollars, and the statement keeps that measure intact.

The 11.3 million-unit estimate in Paragraph 4 matches the statement.

**C) South Korea's 2021 investment programme is described as being funded exclusively by private companies without any public involvement.**

Paragraph 5 calls South Korea's 2021 programme a "$450 billion publicprivate investment programme." "Exclusively… private" and "without any public involvement" erase the public half of that label. The whole paragraph is framed as governments responding with "unusually direct industrial intervention," so a purely private reading also fights the surrounding context, not just the one compound adjective. Absolute words like "exclusively" and "without any" are worth flagging on sight, since they leave no room for the mixed arrangement the text describes.

**Trap:** Public–private becomes private-only — watch the funding mix.

The claim fails; Paragraph 5 marks the programme as public-private, not private-only: "a $450 billion publicprivate investment programme."

**D) Japan is described as having been the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan was "once the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share to competitors." The statement restates that rise-and-loss arc without inventing a new ranking today. The word "once" anchors the dominance firmly in the past, and the statement's past-perfect phrasing "having been" respects that timeline instead of implying present leadership. Both halves of the arc must survive the paraphrase: peak in the 1980s, then significant loss of share.

The 1980s-dominance-then-loss wording in Paragraph 5 confirms the line.

**E) The affected automotive-grade chip category is described as representing a large majority of the overall semiconductor market by value.**

Paragraph 4 says those automotive-grade chips were "worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market." "Large majority" is the inverse of "small fraction." The small share is the entire point of the paragraph, because the contrast between a minor market slice and a massive production loss is what makes the disruption striking. Reading the category as a majority would dissolve that contrast and leave the paragraph's "nonetheless" with nothing to push against.

**Trap:** Small market share ↔ large majority is a quantity swap.

The statement fails; the passage calls the category "worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market," not a large majority.
highlights: A production slowdown affecting a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips
reducing global vehicle production by an estimated 11.3 million units
a $450 billion publicprivate investment programme in 2021
Japan, once the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share to competitors
worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market

tactical_explanations:
**A) The "silicon shield" theory suggests Taiwan's indispensability gives other nations incentive to help ensure its security.**

Paragraph 6 explains the "silicon shield" idea as theorising that Taiwan's indispensability to global electronics supply chains gives other nations a powerful incentive to help ensure its continued security. The statement strips hedging words but keeps the same protective logic. Crucially, it also keeps the attribution: the claim is what the theory suggests, not what the passage asserts as fact, which is why the softer verb "suggests" is acceptable. The causal chain also survives intact — indispensability produces the incentive, and the incentive points toward security.

The shield theory in Paragraph 6 matches the claim.

**B) Critics of the silicon shield theory argue it could make Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one.**

Paragraph 6 immediately counters that the same dynamic "could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one." The statement is that counterargument almost verbatim. It preserves the modal "could" as well as the "rather than" contrast, so the critics' position stays a possible reading instead of hardening into a prediction. Attribution is correct too: the target reading belongs to the critics, not to the analysts who proposed the shield.

The critics' target-vs-protected contrast in Paragraph 6 confirms the line.

**C) Chinese chipmakers, as of the early 2020s, are described as having fully closed the technological gap with the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraph 7 says Chinese manufacturers as of the early 2020s "remained several process-technology generations behind the industry's absolute cutting edge." "Fully closed" contradicts "several… generations behind." The verb "remained" signals a gap that persisted through the stated time window, so the timeframe in the statement is no escape hatch. The passage's whole point in that paragraph is how hard the gap is to close, which the statement inverts into an accomplished catch-up.

**Trap:** Lag in the text becomes catch-up in the statement.

The claim fails; Paragraph 7 reports Chinese makers "remained several process-technology generations behind," not caught up.

**D) Legacy chips are described as irrelevant to critical everyday products such as cars and medical devices.**

Paragraph 8 says legacy chips "remain critical to everyday products such as cars, appliances, and medical devices." "Irrelevant" flips "critical." The examples in the statement are drawn straight from the passage's own list, which makes the surrounding wording feel familiar and disguises the single reversed adjective. Remember that the paragraph exists precisely to argue that unglamorous older chips still matter, so "irrelevant" contradicts its purpose as well as its wording.

The statement fails; the passage says legacy chips "remain critical" to those products, not irrelevant.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting the industry's future concentration as a settled matter with a clear, agreed-upon outcome.**

Paragraph 9 ends by calling whether diversification will reduce concentration — or economics will keep favouring it — "an open question actively debated among industry analysts and policymakers." "Settled" and "agreed-upon" erase that open debate. The closing sentence is built as a two-sided "whether… or whether…" structure, which by design leaves both futures on the table rather than choosing one. Naming the debaters — analysts and policymakers — reinforces that disagreement is ongoing rather than resolved.

**Trap:** An "open question" is dressed up as a closed conclusion.

The claim fails; Paragraph 9 frames the outcome as "an open question actively debated," not a settled consensus.
highlights: theorising that the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains gives other nations a powerful incentive to help ensure its continued security
critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
Chinese manufacturers as of the early 2020s remained several process-technology generations behind the industry's absolute cutting edge
remain critical to everyday products such as cars, appliances, and medical devices
remains an open question actively debated among industry analysts and policymakers

tactical_explanations:
**A) Since ASML is the sole manufacturer of the most advanced lithography machines, it can be inferred that any country lacking access to ASML's equipment would face significant obstacles reaching the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraph 2 calls ASML's monopoly a second, narrower chokepoint layered on TSMC concentration, and the machines are described as essential for etching advanced patterns. If the only maker is ASML, denied access logically blocks the path to the cutting edge. The inference stays modest in its wording — "significant obstacles," not total impossibility — which keeps it inside what a single-supplier bottleneck can support. Paragraph 7 quietly reinforces the same logic by noting that export restrictions on advanced chipmaking equipment left China several generations behind.

**Tip:** A named sole supplier of "essential" gear supports a real barrier inference — stay inside that logic, don't invent extra firms.

The inference follows from ASML's sole-maker chokepoint in Paragraph 2, so the statement holds.

**B) Because rising fab costs have outpaced transistor-density gains under "Moore's Second Law," it can be inferred that entering cutting-edge manufacturing has become relatively more, not less, difficult over time.**

Paragraph 3 says capital costs have risen even faster than transistor doubling, "making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge." "More, not less, difficult" is exactly that progressive-hardening claim. The comparison is relative by design: costs rising "even faster" than density gains is what turns a technical trend into a widening financial barrier. The inference also respects the passage's escape clause, since the text allows entry with "government-scale financial backing" and the statement never claims entry is impossible.

Moore's Second Law in Paragraph 3 supports the inference that entry has gotten harder over time.

**C) Because the chip shortage's automotive impact was disproportionate to that category's market share, it can be inferred that even a narrow, low-value disruption can produce outsized economic consequences.**

Paragraph 4 stresses a relatively narrow, small-fraction automotive category that still idled lines and cut about 11.3 million vehicles. The mismatch between small market share and huge production damage is the disproportion the statement names. Paragraph 8 later states this lesson outright, noting that disruptions "need not involve cutting-edge technology at all to produce outsized economic consequences." An inference that simply generalises a pattern the passage itself draws twice is safe territory.

The narrow-category / outsized-impact pairing in Paragraph 4 backs the inference.

**D) Since China has invested billions in domestic chip production, it can be inferred that state investment alone is sufficient to fully replicate decades of accumulated engineering expertise.**

Paragraph 7 says that despite billions in state investment, China still lagged several generations behind, "illustrating how difficult it is to close this particular technological gap through capital investment alone, without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise." "Sufficient alone" contradicts "not… alone." The passage uses the concessive "despite" precisely to signal that the money did not deliver the outcome, so the spending detail is evidence against the inference rather than for it. The word "alone" appears in both the text and the statement but points in opposite directions, which is what makes the trap convincing.

**Trap:** Heavy spending in the text is twisted into proof that money is enough.

The inference fails; Paragraph 7 denies that capital alone can replace "decades of accumulated engineering expertise."

**E) Because Japan is subsidising new fabrication facilities, it can be inferred that Japan currently holds the largest share of global advanced chip manufacturing.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan is subsidising new fabs to rebuild capability it allowed to atrophy after losing 1980s dominance. Paragraph 1 already assigns more than 90% of the most advanced logic chips to TSMC in Taiwan — not to Japan. Subsidies for recovery do not equal today's lead. The verb "rebuild" presupposes a capability that was lost, which is the opposite of the leading position the inference asserts. Two separate paragraphs therefore block this reading: one places Japan's dominance in the past, the other places today's share with TSMC.

**Trap:** Policy effort today is mistaken for current market leadership.

The inference fails; leadership sits with TSMC's "more than 90%" share, while Japan is described as rebuilding lost ground.
highlights: Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment, creating a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first
the capital cost of the factories needed to manufacture those increasingly dense chips has risen even faster, making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge

tactical_explanations:
**A) The extreme cost and complexity described early in the passage help explain why so few countries or companies can realistically compete at the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraphs 2–3 stack $20 billion fabs, $150 million lithography tools, a single ASML supplier, and Moore's Second Law capital barriers. Those early obstacles are precisely why new entrants struggle at the cutting edge without government-scale backing. Paragraph 2 also opens by insisting the concentration "did not emerge by accident," which signals that the cost details are offered as explanation rather than as background colour. The synthesis simply follows that explanatory arrow from causes in the early paragraphs to the scarcity of competitors.

The early cost-and-complexity stack explains the scarcity of cutting-edge competitors, so the synthesis holds.

**B) The chip shortage's disproportionate impact on vehicle production is consistent with the later point that even legacy, technologically unremarkable chips can cause significant disruption.**

Paragraph 4's automotive shortage hit hard despite a small market slice; Paragraph 8 then notes that even legacy chips remain critical and that disruptions need not involve cutting-edge tech to produce outsized consequences. Both scenes show modest-looking chip classes punching above their technological or market profile. Cars appear in both places — as the industry idled in Paragraph 4 and as an example product in Paragraph 8 — which makes the two passages describe the same vulnerability from two angles. The statement claims only consistency between them, which is exactly the relationship the text sets up.

Linking Paragraph 4's outsized hit to Paragraph 8's legacy-chip warning is a fair cross-section read.

**C) Because South Korea and Japan are both investing in domestic capacity, the passage implies these efforts have already fully resolved the industry's underlying geographic concentration.**

Paragraph 5 reports the investment moves, but Paragraph 9 still leaves whether diversification will reduce concentrated vulnerabilities an "open question actively debated." "Already fully resolved" jumps past that undecided ending. The closing paragraph even asks whether the economics of chipmaking will keep favouring concentration "regardless of policy intervention," which directly anticipates and rejects this reading. Announcements of spending describe intent, not completed structural change, and the passage never reports an outcome for either programme.

**Trap:** Announced policy is treated as a finished fix.

The synthesis fails; Paragraph 9 keeps the outcome an open question, not a resolved one.

**D) The "silicon shield" theory and the critics' counterargument together illustrate that Taiwan's chip dominance carries genuinely contested strategic implications, not a single agreed-upon interpretation.**

Paragraph 6 presents both the protective "silicon shield" reading and the critics' "tempting target" counter. Setting theory and rebuttal side by side signals contested meaning, not consensus. The hedged verbs across the paragraph — "some analysts have described," "theorising," "critics counter" — keep both readings as positions held by people rather than settled findings. That is exactly the contested-implications picture the statement describes.

The paired theory-and-critique in Paragraph 6 supports a contested-implications reading.

**E) Because China remains several generations behind despite heavy investment, this is consistent with the earlier point that capital cost alone does not guarantee competitive success at the cutting edge.**

Paragraph 3 says rising capital costs make cutting-edge entry progressively harder without government-scale backing and, by implication, more than money. Paragraph 7 shows China still generations behind despite billions, needing decades of engineering expertise too. The later lag illustrates the earlier capital-is-not-enough barrier. China's case is effectively the test that the earlier principle predicted: government-scale money was present, yet the gap persisted. Reading the two paragraphs together turns an economic claim into a documented example rather than a contradiction.

China's lag under heavy spending lines up with the earlier capital-barrier logic, so the synthesis holds.

tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the shortage not disrupted automotive supply chains, vehicle production would have remained substantially higher."**

This is a third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + past participle replaces If… had. The result clause correctly uses would have + past participle (would have remained). The negation sits on the inverted had-clause without breaking the pattern. Note that the inverted form takes no if at all — writing "If had the shortage not disrupted…" would double the marker and spoil the structure. Both clauses also point at the same unreal past, which is what the third conditional is built to express.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… not… pairs with would have + V3 — same timeline as If… had not…

The conditional architecture is sound, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Regulators recommended that the company diversifies its supplier base to reduce risk."**

After recommend that, formal English wants the mandative subjunctive — base form diversify, not present-tense diversifies. The -s ending treats the verb as an ordinary present instead of a subjunctive. The subjunctive form stays the same no matter what tense the reporting verb carries, so "recommended" in the past does not pull the that-clause into agreement with it. The same rule governs verbs such as suggest, insist, demand, and propose, which is worth memorising as a family.

**Trap:** Recommend that + indicative -s is a frequent near-miss.

The line fails; the repaired wording is "Regulators recommended that the company diversify its supplier base to reduce risk."

**C) "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continue to increase each year."**

The number of is grammatically singular, so the verb must be continues, not plural continue. The plural countries after of does not control agreement. The head noun is number, and the of-phrase together with the participial modifier subsidising domestic fabs only describes it. Contrast this with a number of, which is idiomatically plural and would take continue — the article alone decides the verb.

**Trap:** A plural noun after of does not make "the number of" plural.

Agreement breaks here; the sound version is "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continues to increase each year."

**D) "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required were easily replicated by new entrants."**

With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here that subject is the expertise required — singular uncountable expertise — so the verb should be was, not were. The past participle required is a reduced relative modifying expertise, so it adds no plural noun that could take over agreement. If the order were reversed to "Neither the expertise nor the equipment…," the nearer noun would still be uncountable and the verb would stay singular.

**Trap:** Two nouns before the verb tempt a plural even when the nearer head is singular.

Proximity agreement fails, so the sentence doesn’t hold — "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required was easily replicated by new entrants."

**E) "Having invested heavily in domestic capacity, the government sought greater supply chain independence."**

The perfect participle Having invested modifies the government, the same agent that sought independence afterward. No dangling or mismatched subject — the investor and the seeker are one. The perfect form also fixes the order of events, marking the investment as complete before the search for independence. A participial opener is only safe when the noun immediately after the comma is its true subject, and that condition is met here.

The participle attaches cleanly to the government, so the wording is sound.

**A) "No sooner had the shortage begun than automakers started idling assembly lines."**

No sooner… than correctly triggers inversion (had the shortage begun) with past perfect in the first clause and simple past (started) in the second. The correlative pair is than, not when. Because No sooner is a negative adverbial placed at the front, the inversion is required rather than optional — "No sooner the shortage had begun" would be wrong. The tense split also carries meaning, marking the first event as just barely complete when the second followed.

**Tip:** No sooner + inversion wants than, and past perfect before the simple-past follow-on.

The No sooner… than pattern is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The programme, along with several related subsidies, were announced the same year."**

Along with several related subsidies is a parenthetical add-on; the real subject is singular the programme, so the verb must be was announced, not were. The plural noun inside the aside does not take over agreement. The paired commas are the giveaway: material fenced off that way can be lifted out, leaving "The programme … was announced the same year." Phrases such as together with, as well as, and in addition to behave identically and never convert a singular subject into a plural one.

**Trap:** Along with + plural looks like a plural subject, but the head noun still governs the verb.

Agreement fails; repair to "The programme, along with several related subsidies, was announced the same year."

**C) "Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported ongoing supply constraints."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when the of-phrase is plural. Have reported should be has reported. The pronoun Each picks out members one at a time, which is why the grammar stays singular even though the group described is plural. The same singular rule covers every one of, either of, and neither of, so treat this whole family as singular by default.

**Trap:** Manufacturers after of invites plural have, but Each keeps the verb singular.

The plural verb after Each is wrong — "Each of the surveyed manufacturers has reported ongoing supply constraints."

**D) "By the time the new fab opens, competitors will have already expanded their own capacity."**

By the time + present (opens) sets a future reference point; will have expanded is future perfect for completion before that point. Already sits naturally inside the perfect. English deliberately uses the present tense after time conjunctions such as by the time, when, and until, so "By the time the new fab will open" would be the error to watch for. The two clauses therefore divide the labour cleanly: one fixes the deadline, the other reports what is finished by then.

Future perfect before a future By the time marker is the right tense pairing, so the line holds.

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across several fiscal years, indicate a persistent cost increase."**

Plural figures takes were compiled in the non-restrictive which-clause and plural indicate in the main clause. Relative and main verbs both track the same plural head. The commas around the which-clause correctly mark it as extra information, and which is the right relative pronoun for that non-restrictive use. Removing the clause leaves "The figures indicate a persistent cost increase," which confirms the main-clause agreement on its own.

Plural subject and plural verbs align throughout, so the sentence is sound.

**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "reckless" means carefully considered and prudent, rather than dangerously risky.**

Paragraph 1 says such geographic concentration "would be considered reckless in almost any other critical industry." There reckless means dangerously unwise or unduly risky — the opposite of carefully considered and prudent. The surrounding sentence is a criticism of how narrowly production is clustered, so a complimentary gloss would clash with the judgement the paragraph is making. The conditional framing "would be considered… in almost any other industry" reinforces that the word carries disapproval.

**Trap:** A negative evaluative word is glossed as its positive antonym.

The gloss fails; in Paragraph 1 reckless means dangerously risky, not prudent.

**B) As used in Paragraph 2, "chokepoint" means a critical point of vulnerability where disruption could severely restrict an entire system.**

Paragraph 2 calls ASML's monopoly "a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first," after describing essential lithography gear only one firm can make. That usage matches a critical vulnerability node whose disruption can bottleneck a whole supply chain. The modifiers do the defining work here: "narrower" and "layered on top of" describe a passage that can be squeezed, which is the metaphor the word carries. Reading the surrounding sentence about a single supplier of essential equipment confirms the bottleneck sense.

The Paragraph 2 sense of chokepoint matches the offered meaning, so the identification holds.

**C) As used in Paragraph 5, "atrophy" means to strengthen and grow steadily over time.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan is trying to rebuild capability "it had allowed to atrophy." Allowed to atrophy means allowed to wither or weaken from disuse — not strengthen and grow. The verb rebuild in the same clause is decisive, since nothing that had been strengthening would need rebuilding. The word also fits the paragraph's earlier note that Japan lost significant market share after its 1980s peak.

The gloss reverses the verb; atrophy here means weaken from neglect, so the meaning claim fails.

**D) As used in Paragraph 6, "indispensability" means the quality of being easily replaced or unnecessary.**

Paragraph 6 speaks of "the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains" as the basis of a silicon-shield theory. Indispensability means being essential / hard to do without — the opposite of easily replaced or unnecessary. The theory only works because the quality is essentialness: nations would have no incentive to protect a supplier they could swap out at will. The prefix in- plus dispensable literally marks something that cannot be dispensed with.

The antonym gloss collapses; indispensability here means essentialness, not replaceability.

**E) As used in Paragraph 8, "outsized" means smaller than would normally be expected.**

Paragraph 8 says disruptions need not involve cutting-edge tech "to produce outsized economic consequences." Outsized means disproportionately large, not smaller than expected. The sentence is built on a contrast between unremarkable technology and the scale of the damage it can cause, which only lands if the consequences are oversized. Paragraph 4's earlier example — a small market slice costing 11.3 million vehicles — shows the same word doing the same work.

**Trap:** Out- as a size prefix is misread as undersized.

The meaning claim fails; outsized here means larger than normal, not smaller.
highlights: creating a level of geographic concentration that would be considered reckless in almost any other critical industry
creating a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first
rebuild capability it had allowed to atrophy
the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains
to produce outsized economic consequences

tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 3, "cutting-edge" means outdated or technologically behind current standards.**

Paragraph 3 talks about competing "at the cutting edge" of chip manufacturing after describing denser, more expensive fabs. Cutting-edge means at the technological forefront — the opposite of outdated or behind. Paragraph 7 makes the same sense visible from the other side, describing Chinese makers as generations behind "the industry's absolute cutting edge," which only reads sensibly if the cutting edge is the front. Paragraph 8's contrast between legacy nodes and cutting-edge technology points the same way.

The gloss fails; cutting-edge here means leading-tech, not behind the curve.

**B) As used in Paragraph 4, "idle" (as in "idle assembly lines") means to keep running continuously at full capacity.**

Paragraph 4 says the shortage "forced automakers worldwide to idle assembly lines," then cut vehicle output by millions. Idle here means shut down or leave unused — not run at full capacity. The consequence clause settles it: production fell by an estimated 11.3 million units, which cannot follow from lines running flat out. Note also that idle is used as a transitive verb here, meaning to render idle, not to describe an engine ticking over.

**Trap:** Everyday "idle" as "not working" is flipped into continuous full production.

The claimed meaning reverses the verb; idle here means stop or pause the lines, so the identification fails.

**C) As used in Paragraph 7, "replicating" means copying or reproducing something that already exists elsewhere.**

Paragraph 7 says closing the gap needs more than capital, "without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise." Replicating there means copying / reproducing that expertise — matching the offered gloss. The object of the verb is expertise built up elsewhere over decades, so the sense is reproducing an existing achievement rather than inventing something new. That is precisely why the paragraph treats it as so hard to do quickly.

The Paragraph 7 use of replicating matches "copying or reproducing," so the meaning holds.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "unremarkable" means ordinary or unexceptional, not attracting special notice.**

Paragraph 8 calls older-node chips "technologically unremarkable by industry standards" — ordinary relative to the cutting edge, not specially impressive. That is ordinary / unexceptional. The qualifier "by industry standards" limits the judgement to technical novelty, which is why the same chips can be unremarkable and critical in the very same sentence. Ordinary, in this context, is a comment on sophistication rather than on importance.

Unremarkable in Paragraph 8 means ordinary, so the identification stands.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "concentration" (in this economic sense) means being spread evenly and widely across many locations.**

Paragraph 9 asks whether economics will "continue to favour concentration" versus geographic diversification. Concentration here means clustering production narrowly — the opposite of even, wide distribution.
